title: LLM Inference Challenges - Understanding Inference Metrics
author: Anurag Mohan

blocks.text: LLM Inference Challenges (Part 15)
Understanding Inference Metrics
In the previous parts, we built a mental model for modern LLM inference systems.
We covered:

KV cache → Part 1 
Memory challenges → Part 2 
GPU utilization and batching → Part 3 
Multi-GPU inference → Parts 4, Part 5, Part 6, Part 7
Distributed serving and routing → Part 8 
GPU communication and networking → Part 9 
Prefill vs Decode → Part 10 
Continuous batching → Part 11 
PagedAttention → Part 12 
vLLM architecture → Part 13 
CUDA, PyTorch, vLLM, CPU inference, routing, and agents → Part 14
At this point, the system picture is much clearer.
But once we understand how inference works, the next question becomes:
How do we know if the inference system is working well?
That leads us to inference metrics.
Why do inference metrics matter?
Until now, we were mostly building intuition.
But real systems need measurement.
Metrics help answer questions like:

Are users waiting too long?
Is the GPU actually being used well?
Is batching working?
Is prefill slow?
Is decode slow?
Is KV cache memory becoming the bottleneck?
Are queues building up?
Can the system handle more users?
Did our latest change improve performance or hurt it?
Without metrics, we are mostly guessing.
With metrics, we can start observing the system.
What does the user experience look like?
From the user’s point of view, inference feels simple:

send prompt
wait for response to start
watch tokens stream
receive final answer
So the user mostly experiences two things:

how long it takes before the first token appears
how fast the remaining tokens continue appearing
These map to two important metrics:

Time To First Token
Inter-token latency
What is Time To First Token?
Time To First Token is usually written as:
TTFT
It means:
how long the user waits before the first generated token appears
Example:

user sends request at 10:00:00.000
first token appears at 10:00:01.200
TTFT = 1.2 seconds
TTFT is important because it controls the first impression.
If TTFT is high, the system feels slow even if the rest of the answer streams quickly.
What happens before the first token?
Before the first token appears, several things happen:

request arrives
request may wait in a queue
scheduler admits the request
prompt is tokenized
prefill runs
KV cache is created
first decode step runs
first token is produced
A simple mental model:
TTFT = queue time + prefill time + first decode step + system overhead
This connects directly to Prefill vs Decode, which we covered in Part 10.
Why can TTFT become high?
TTFT can increase because of:

long prompts
high queue time
overloaded replicas
slow prefill
limited KV cache memory
scheduler delays
too many active requests
traffic spikes
So when TTFT is high, the better question is not:
Why is the model slow?
The better question is:
Where is the time being spent?
What is inter-token latency?
After the first token appears, generation continues token by token.
Inter-token latency means:
how much time passes between generated tokens
Example:

token 1 appears
100 ms later, token 2 appears
100 ms later, token 3 appears
Inter-token latency is roughly:
100 ms per token
This metric tells us how smooth the streaming experience feels.
Why is inter-token latency connected to decode?
After prefill, the system enters decode.
Decode generates one token at a time:

token 1
token 2
token 3
token 4
Each token depends on the previous token.
So inter-token latency is mostly connected to decode speed.
Can TTFT be good while inter-token latency is bad?
Yes.
A system can start quickly but stream slowly.
Example:

TTFT = good
inter-token latency = bad
This usually means:

request admission was fast
prefill was acceptable
but decode is slow
Possible causes:

small active batch
memory bandwidth pressure
KV cache access overhead
communication overhead
inefficient scheduling during decode
This connects to continuous batching, which we covered in Part 11.
Can TTFT be bad while inter-token latency is good?
Yes.
A request can wait a long time before starting, but stream quickly once it begins.
Example:

TTFT = 5 seconds
inter-token latency = 50 ms
This may indicate:

queueing problem
long prefill
scheduler pressure
KV cache memory pressure
overloaded serving replica
So TTFT and inter-token latency tell different stories.
We need both.
What is total request latency?
Total request latency means:
time from request arrival to final token
It includes:

queue time
prefill
decode
streaming
final completion
A simple mental model:
Total latency = TTFT + time to generate remaining tokens
But total latency can be misleading.
Why?
Because output length matters.
A request generating 20 tokens and a request generating 1000 tokens should not be compared directly without context.
So total latency should be interpreted together with:

input tokens
output tokens
TTFT
inter-token latency
concurrency level
What is throughput?
Throughput means:
how much useful work the system completes over time
For LLM inference, this is usually measured as:
tokens per second
Example:

system generates 10,000 output tokens in 10 seconds
throughput = 1000 tokens/sec
Throughput matters because inference systems usually serve many users.
Higher throughput usually means:

more users served
better GPU efficiency
lower cost per token
better batching efficiency
What kinds of throughput should we track?
There are a few useful throughput metrics:

Output tokens/sec
Input tokens/sec
Total tokens/sec
Requests/sec
Tokens/sec is usually more meaningful than requests/sec because LLM requests vary a lot.
One request may generate 10 tokens.
Another may generate 1000 tokens.
So request count alone does not describe system load very well.
Why separate input and output tokens?
Because prefill and decode behave differently.
Prefill processes input tokens.
Decode generates output tokens.
Example workloads:

long prompt + short answer
short prompt + long answer
long prompt + long answer
many short chat requests
Each workload stresses the system differently.
So we should ask:

Are we measuring prefill throughput?
Are we measuring decode throughput?
Are we measuring total throughput?
This again connects to Part 10 — Prefill vs Decode.
What is queue time?
Queue time means:
how long a request waits before the inference engine starts processing it
Queue time affects TTFT directly.
Queue time can grow when:

too many requests arrive
active batch is full
KV cache memory is limited
GPU workers are busy
prefill workload is large
scheduler cannot admit new requests quickly
Queue time is often one of the clearest signs that demand is exceeding capacity.
What is batch size?
Batch size means:
how many requests or tokens are processed together
In LLM inference, batching can mean different things:

number of active requests
number of active sequences
number of tokens processed in a step
number of prefill tokens
number of decode tokens
The simple intuition:

larger batches usually improve GPU utilization
but larger batches can increase waiting time
This is the latency-throughput tradeoff we covered in Part 11 — Continuous Batching.
What is batch occupancy?
Batch occupancy means:
how full the active batch is compared to what the system can handle
Example:

system can efficiently handle 32 active decode requests
currently running only 8 active decode requests
batch occupancy is low
Low batch occupancy can mean:

GPU is not receiving enough work
throughput may be low
batching is not effective
This matters especially during decode because each request only contributes one token of work at a time.
Why does batch occupancy matter during decode?
During decode:

each active request generates one token
each decode step is relatively small
GPU efficiency depends on having enough active requests
Example:
Batch = [A]
The system runs a decode step for one request.
Now compare:
Batch = [A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H]
The system still runs a decode step, but many users receive tokens.
That is why continuous batching tries to keep the active batch full.
What is GPU utilization?
GPU utilization tells us how busy the GPU is.
Simple mental model:

high GPU utilization = GPU is actively doing work
low GPU utilization = GPU is waiting or underused
This matters because GPUs are expensive.
If utilization is low, we may be paying for hardware that is not doing enough useful work.
Is high GPU utilization always good?
Not always.
High GPU utilization can mean the system is efficient.
But it can also mean the system is overloaded.
Example:

GPU utilization = 99%
queue time = high
TTFT = bad
p99 latency = bad
That means the GPU is busy, but users are waiting too long.
So GPU utilization must be read together with:

TTFT
queue time
throughput
p95/p99 latency
error rate
Is low GPU utilization always bad?
Not always.
Low utilization may be fine during low traffic.
But low utilization during high traffic can indicate a problem.
Possible causes:

batches are too small
scheduler is not filling batches
requests are spread across too many replicas
CPU bottleneck
tokenization bottleneck
network bottleneck
memory bottleneck
communication overhead
So utilization only makes sense with workload context.
What is GPU memory utilization?
GPU memory is used for:

model weights
KV cache
activations
temporary buffers
runtime overhead
Model weights are mostly fixed after loading.
KV cache grows with:

active requests
prompt length
generated tokens
context window size
So GPU memory utilization tells us how much memory capacity is still available.
What is KV cache utilization?
KV cache utilization tells us:
how much KV cache memory is currently occupied
This is important because KV cache often limits concurrency.
If KV cache utilization is high:

fewer new requests can enter
active batch size may be limited
queue time may increase
TTFT may increase
throughput may stop improving
This connects directly to:

Part 1 — KV Cache 
Part 2 — Memory Challenges 
Part 12 — PagedAttention
Why can KV cache limit concurrency?
Every active request needs KV cache.
Longer sequences need more cache.
Example:

Request A → 500 tokens
Request B → 4000 tokens
Request C → 8000 tokens
As active sequences grow, KV cache memory fills up.
Eventually, the system may have compute capacity but not enough memory to admit more requests.
This is one of the most important inference lessons:

LLM inference is not only compute-limited.
It can also be memory-limited.
Why does this connect to PagedAttention?
PagedAttention helps manage KV cache memory more efficiently.
The key idea from Part 12 :

KV cache is split into fixed-size blocks
blocks do not need to be physically contiguous
requests can grow dynamically
finished requests return blocks to the pool
memory fragmentation becomes less harmful
So when KV cache utilization is high, we start seeing why memory management matters so much.
What are p50, p95, and p99?
Average latency is not enough.
We also need percentiles.
Common latency percentiles:
These help us understand tail latency.
Why does tail latency matter?
Tail latency shows the slow cases.
Example:

p50 TTFT = 500 ms
p99 TTFT = 12 seconds
This means most users are fine, but some users wait a very long time.
For production systems, p95 and p99 matter because users often remember the bad cases.
Tail latency can increase because of:

long prompts
large outputs
traffic spikes
queue buildup
memory pressure
scheduler delays
replica imbalance
network issues
What is error rate?
Error rate tells us how often requests fail.
Failures may include:

timeouts
out-of-memory errors
server errors
cancelled requests
rate limit errors
model worker crashes
unhealthy replicas
A fast system is not useful if it fails often.
So error rate is an important operational metric.
What is timeout rate?
Timeout rate tells us how often requests take too long and get cancelled or rejected.
Timeouts may happen because:

queues are too long
responses are too long
replica is overloaded
model worker is stuck
network call is slow
system capacity is too low
Timeouts usually mean latency has become bad enough to break the user experience.
What is cost per token?
Cost per token means:
how much it costs to process or generate each token
Simple mental model:
GPU cost / tokens generated = cost per token
This is where inference metrics become business metrics.
If throughput improves while hardware cost stays the same:

cost per token goes down
GPU usage becomes more efficient
serving economics improve
This is why batching, scheduling, and memory efficiency matter.
They are not just technical optimizations.
They directly affect cost.
How do these metrics connect to earlier concepts?
A useful mapping:
This table helped me connect the conceptual articles to real system operations.
What does an overloaded system look like?
An overloaded inference system may show:

queue time increasing
TTFT increasing
p95/p99 latency getting worse
KV cache utilization near limit
GPU utilization very high
timeout rate increasing
error rate increasing
Possible fixes:

add more replicas
improve routing
reduce max context length
reduce max output tokens
use a smaller model
improve batching
improve KV cache efficiency
autoscale earlier
What does an underutilized system look like?
An underutilized system may show:

low GPU utilization
low batch occupancy
low throughput
good latency
This may be fine during low traffic.
But if traffic is high, possible causes include:

requests spread across too many replicas
batch sizes too small
scheduler not filling batches
routing is inefficient
workload is too fragmented
This is the other side of the latency-throughput tradeoff.
What does a memory-limited system look like?
A memory-limited system may show:

high GPU memory usage
high KV cache utilization
limited ability to admit new requests
queue time increasing
batch size capped
GPU compute not fully used
This is where the system may have compute available but still cannot serve more users because memory is the bottleneck.
What does a decode bottleneck look like?
A decode bottleneck may show:

TTFT is acceptable
tokens stream slowly
inter-token latency is high
decode throughput is low
active requests keep running for a long time
GPU utilization may be uneven
Possible causes:

small active batches
KV cache access overhead
memory bandwidth pressure
communication overhead
too many long-running requests
This is why continuous batching matters.
What does a prefill bottleneck look like?
A prefill bottleneck may show:

TTFT is high
long prompts are especially slow
input tokens/sec is low
queue time may increase
decode may be fine after generation starts
This often happens with:

long documents
long RAG contexts
large prompts
many new requests arriving together
Why is workload shape important?
Metrics only make sense if we understand the workload.
Important workload dimensions:

prompt length
output length
concurrency
model size
context window
streaming vs non-streaming
sampling parameters
hardware type
number of replicas
quantization level
Example:

short prompts + short outputs
short prompts + long outputs
long prompts + short outputs
long prompts + long outputs
Each workload stresses the system differently.
So benchmark numbers without workload details are not very useful.
What should a good benchmark mention?
A useful benchmark should include:

model name
model size
hardware
serving engine
number of GPUs
quantization
prompt length
output length
concurrency level
streaming or non-streaming
measured metrics
p50/p95/p99 values
any important config settings
Without these details, performance numbers are hard to compare.
What is the simplest metric set to start with?
For the first hands-on experiment, I would start with:

TTFT
inter-token latency
total request latency
output tokens/sec
requests/sec
GPU utilization
GPU memory usage
Then later add:

queue time
KV cache utilization
batch occupancy
p50/p95/p99 latency
error rate
cost per token
The goal is not to measure everything on day one.
The goal is to start connecting concepts to real observations.
How does this connect to LLMOps?
This is where inference becomes operational.
LLMOps is not only:
deploy the model
It is also:

monitor the model service
understand latency
watch GPU usage
detect queue buildup
track failures
understand cost
scale replicas
debug bottlenecks
compare serving configurations
So inference metrics are the bridge between:
understanding inference systems
and
operating inference systems
What is the key mental model?
I would summarize inference metrics like this:

TTFT
Inter-token latency
Throughput
Queue time
GPU utilization
GPU memory utilization
KV cache utilization
Batch occupancy
p95/p99 latency
Error rate
Cost per token
Together, these metrics tell us whether the inference system is healthy.
Why this article matters
Until now, I was mostly asking:
How does inference work?
Now the question becomes:
How do we observe inference working?
That is a big shift.
Because real inference engineering is not only about knowing the concepts.
It is also about:

measuring behavior
finding bottlenecks
understanding tradeoffs
improving latency
improving throughput
reducing cost
keeping the system reliable
This is where the learning starts moving from mental models into hands-on systems work.
What comes next?
Now that the key inference metrics are clearer, the next step is to measure them in a real serving system.
So the next part will be: Running vLLM Locally and Measuring Inference Metrics
This is also a good point to start a small GitHub repo.
The goal is not to build a perfect benchmarking system immediately.
The goal is to start building intuition from real measurements.
Because once we can measure the system, we can finally start experimenting with it.
